A cell that has its genetic material enclosed in a nucleus. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic cells; they also have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.

A cell whose genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus. Bacterial cells are prokaryotic cells: they have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall, they are much smaller than plant and animal cells, and their genetic material is a single DNA loop.
A small ring of DNA in the cytoplasm of a bacterial cell, separate from the single DNA loop. A bacterial cell may contain one or more plasmids.
The sub-cellular structure that encloses the genetic material of a plant or animal cell and controls the activities of the cell.
The structure that surrounds the cytoplasm of a cell and controls the passage of substances into and out of the cell.
The jelly-like part of a cell in which most of the cell's chemical reactions take place and in which the sub-cellular structures are found.

Sub-cellular structures in which aerobic respiration takes place, transferring the energy the cell needs to carry out its functions. Cells that need a great deal of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.
Sub-cellular structures where protein synthesis takes place: amino acids are joined together to make the proteins the cell needs.

A sub-cellular structure found in plant and algal cells that contains chlorophyll. The chlorophyll absorbs light so that the cell can carry out photosynthesis, so chloroplasts are found in plant cells that receive light rather than in every plant cell.
A space in the cytoplasm of a plant cell that is filled with cell sap. It is one of the parts plant cells often have in addition to the parts found in animal cells.
A layer made of cellulose that surrounds the cell membrane of plant and algal cells and strengthens the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall.
A cell whose structure enables it to carry out a particular function. Examples are sperm cells, nerve cells and muscle cells in animals, and root hair cells, xylem and phloem cells in plants.
A specialised plant cell in the root with a long, thin extension into the soil. The extension increases the surface area of the cell for absorbing water and mineral ions.

Specialised plant cells that form transport tissues. Xylem cells form hollow tubes with thickened walls that carry water and mineral ions from the roots; phloem cells form tubes with sieve plates that carry dissolved sugars through the plant.

The process in which a cell acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function, so that it becomes a specialised cell. Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage, while many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
How many times larger an image is than the real object, calculated using magnification = size of image / size of real object. The image size and the real size must be measured in the same units.

The ability of a microscope to show two points that are close together as separate points. An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope, so it can be used to study cells in much finer detail.

The simple cell division by which bacteria multiply. If they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature, bacteria can divide as often as once every 20 minutes, so the population doubles at each division.
The nutrients supplied for growing microorganisms. Bacteria can be grown in a nutrient broth solution, or as colonies on an agar gel plate.

The set of precautions used to prepare an uncontaminated culture. Petri dishes and culture media are sterilised before use; inoculating loops are sterilised by passing them through a flame; the lid of the Petri dish is secured with adhesive tape and the dish is stored upside down; and in school and college laboratories cultures are incubated at a maximum temperature of 25°C.

A culture that contains only the microorganism being studied, with no microorganisms from the air, the skin or the apparatus. Uncontaminated cultures are required for investigating the action of disinfectants and antibiotics.
A structure found in the nucleus of a cell, made of a DNA molecule. Each chromosome carries a large number of genes.
A section of a DNA molecule carried on a chromosome. A single chromosome carries a large number of genes, so genes are much smaller structures than chromosomes.
Pairs of chromosomes in body cells
In body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs, so each type of chromosome is present twice in the nucleus.

The series of stages in which cells divide. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells. The three overall stages are growth with DNA replication, mitosis, and division of the cytoplasm and cell membranes.
Growth stage of the cell cycle

Before a cell can divide it needs to grow and increase the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. In this stage the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
The stage of the cell cycle in which one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
Division of the cytoplasm and cell membranes
The final stage of the cell cycle, in which the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.
Cell division by mitosis is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms, because it produces new cells that are identical to the parent cell.
An undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.
Stem cells from human embryos, which can be cloned and made to differentiate into most different types of human cells.
Adult stem cells in bone marrow
Stem cells from adult bone marrow, which can form many types of cells including blood cells.
Tissue in plants that can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the life of the plant.
A process in which an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient. Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body so they may be used for medical treatment.

Stem cells from meristems in plants can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically. Rare species can be cloned to protect them from extinction, and crop plants with special features such as disease resistance can be cloned to produce large numbers of identical plants for farmers.

The spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Substances may move into and out of cells across the cell membranes via diffusion, and no energy from respiration is needed.

The difference in concentrations of a substance between two areas. Diffusion gives a net movement down a concentration gradient, from the area of higher concentration to the area of lower concentration; the greater the difference in concentrations, the faster the rate of diffusion.
Factors affecting the rate of diffusion

The factors which affect the rate of diffusion are the difference in concentrations (concentration gradient), the temperature, and the surface area of the membrane. Increasing any one of these increases the rate of diffusion.

Substances transported in and out of cells by diffusion include oxygen and carbon dioxide in gas exchange, and the waste product urea, which moves from cells into the blood plasma for excretion in the kidney.

The surface area of an organism or cell compared with its volume. A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, which allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism. The ratio gets smaller as an organism gets larger.

A surface in a multicellular organism that is specialised for exchanging materials, so that sufficient molecules can be transported into and out of cells for the organism's needs. Its effectiveness is increased by having a large surface area, a membrane that is thin, (in animals) an efficient blood supply and, in animals for gaseous exchange, being ventilated.
The short distance a substance has to travel across an exchange surface. A membrane that is thin provides a short diffusion path, which increases the effectiveness of the exchange surface.

The small intestine and lungs in mammals, gills in fish, and the roots and leaves in plants are adapted for exchange by having a large surface area and a thin membrane that gives a short diffusion path. The small intestine, lungs and gills also have an efficient blood supply, and the lungs are ventilated.
The diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. Water may move across cell membranes via osmosis.
A membrane that allows water molecules through but not all of the dissolved solute particles. Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane.
The movement of substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, that is against a concentration gradient. This requires energy from respiration.
Mineral ion uptake by root hairs
Active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hairs from very dilute solutions in the soil, against a concentration gradient. Plants require ions for healthy growth.
Active transport allows sugar molecules to be absorbed from lower concentrations in the gut into the blood, which has a higher sugar concentration. Sugar molecules are used for cell respiration.
The basic building block from which all living organisms are made.
A group of cells with a similar structure and function.
An aggregation of tissues performing specific functions.
A group of organs that organs are organised into; organ systems work together to form organisms.
An organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food.
A large protein molecule that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up a reaction in a living organism without being changed by it.
The part of an enzyme molecule that the substrate fits into. Its shape means the enzyme catalyses only one specific reaction.
A simplified model of enzyme action in which the substrate (the key) fits into the active site of the enzyme (the lock).
The change in the shape of an enzyme's active site caused by a high temperature or the wrong pH, so that the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.
The sum of all the reactions in a cell or in the body. These reactions are catalysed by enzymes.
The breakdown of food by digestive enzymes into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
A carbohydrase is an enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates to simple sugars. Amylase is a carbohydrase which breaks down starch.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins to amino acids.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.
Sites of production of digestive enzymes

Amylase is produced in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine. Protease is produced in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine. Lipase is produced in the pancreas and the small intestine.
The small soluble molecules produced by digestion. They are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.

An alkaline liquid made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It neutralises hydrochloric acid from the stomach and emulsifies fat to form small droplets, which increases the surface area. The alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.
An organ that pumps blood around the body. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, where gas exchange takes place, and the left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.
A circulation in which the blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body: once on the way to the lungs and once on the way to the rest of the body.
Blood vessels associated with the heart

The vena cava carries blood into the heart from the body and the pulmonary artery carries blood from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries blood from the lungs back to the heart and the aorta carries blood from the heart to the body. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself.
Air passes down the trachea, into the bronchi and then into the alveoli, which are surrounded by a capillary network.
The tiny air sacs of the lungs, adapted for gaseous exchange by a large surface area, thin walls and the capillary network that surrounds them.
A group of cells located in the right atrium that controls the natural resting heart rate. Artificial pacemakers are electrical devices used to correct irregularities in the heart rate.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Its wall is thick, containing muscle and elastic fibres, so that it withstands the high pressure of the blood.
A blood vessel that carries blood back towards the heart. Its wall is thin and it contains valves, because the blood is at low pressure.
A very narrow blood vessel with a wall one cell thick, so that substances can pass quickly between the blood and the tissues.
A tissue consisting of plasma, in which the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended.
The liquid part of the blood, which transports the blood cells and dissolved substances around the body.
A blood cell that carries oxygen. It contains haemoglobin, has no nucleus and is a biconcave disc, giving a large surface area for the uptake of oxygen.
A blood cell that defends the body against pathogens, for example by engulfing them or by producing antibodies.
A small fragment of cell suspended in the plasma that helps the blood to clot at a wound.

A disease in which layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them. This reduces the flow of blood through the coronary arteries, resulting in a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle.
Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open. Statins are widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.
A heart valve that does not open fully, or that develops a leak, so that less blood is pumped or blood flows the wrong way. Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves.

In the case of heart failure a donor heart, or heart and lungs, can be transplanted. Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.
The state of physical and mental well-being.
Communicable diseases can be passed from one person to another, while non-communicable diseases cannot. Both are major causes of ill health.

Different types of disease may interact, for example defects in the immune system make infectious disease more likely, viruses living in cells can trigger cancers, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.
Something that is linked to an increased rate of a disease. Risk factors can be aspects of a person's lifestyle, or substances in the person's body or environment.

An explanation of how a risk factor brings about a disease. A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others, and many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.
Choosing a sample that is large enough and representative of the whole population, so that conclusions drawn from scientific data, including epidemiological data, are reliable.
The result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.

Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells which are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and do not invade other parts of the body. Malignant tumour cells are cancers: they invade neighbouring tissues and spread to different parts of the body in the blood, where they form secondary tumours.
Lifestyle risk factors have been identified for various types of cancer, and there are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.

Knowledge of the digestive system from Key Stage 3 science is assumed: food passes through the mouth, stomach and small intestine, where it is broken down, and the small soluble products are absorbed in the small intestine.

A reaction written using the names of the substances rather than formulae, for example starch to sugars, or lipids to glycerol and fatty acids. Simple word equations should be understood; no chemical symbol equations are required.
The tissue that covers the outer surfaces of a plant. In a leaf it forms the upper and lower epidermis, a protective covering that contains the guard cells surrounding the stomata.
The leaf tissue lying just below the upper epidermis. Its closely packed cells contain many chloroplasts, so this is the main tissue in which photosynthesis takes place.
The leaf tissue lying below the palisade mesophyll. Its cells are loosely packed with air spaces between them, so gases can diffuse to and from the photosynthesising cells.
Plant tissue found at the growing tips of shoots and roots. Its cells divide to produce the new cells a plant needs for growth.

The tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. It is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, adapted for the transport of water in the transpiration stream.

The tissue that transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage. It is composed of tubes of elongated cells, and cell sap can move from one phloem cell to the next through pores in the end walls.
The movement of food molecules, as dissolved sugars, through phloem tissue from the leaves to the rest of the plant.

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, which diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata. The transpiration stream is the movement of water taken up by the roots and carried up through the xylem to the stems and leaves that replaces it.
A cell on the outside of a root, drawn out into a long thin hair that gives a large surface area. It is adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis and of mineral ions by active transport.
A stoma is a pore in the epidermis of a leaf. Each stoma is surrounded by a pair of guard cells that open and close it. The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss.
The roots, stem and leaves, which work together as an organ system for the transport of substances around the plant.
A microorganism that causes infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. They may infect plants or animals and can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air.
rapid reproduction of pathogens in the body
Bacteria and viruses may reproduce rapidly inside the body, so the number of pathogens present can rise quickly after an infection begins.
A poison that bacteria may produce. Toxins damage tissues and make us feel ill.
Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage. This is how a viral infection harms the body, rather than by producing toxins.

A viral disease showing symptoms of fever and a red skin rash. The measles virus is spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs. Measles is a serious illness that can be fatal if complications arise, and for this reason most young children are vaccinated against measles.

HIV is a virus that initially causes a flu-like illness and is spread by sexual contact or exchange of body fluids such as blood, which occurs when drug users share needles. Unless successfully controlled with antiretroviral drugs the virus attacks the body's immune cells. Late stage HIV infection, or AIDS, occurs when the body's immune system becomes so badly damaged it can no longer deal with other infections or cancers.

A widespread plant pathogen affecting many species of plants including tomatoes. It gives a distinctive 'mosaic' pattern of discolouration on the leaves which affects the growth of the plant due to lack of photosynthesis.

A bacterial disease spread by bacteria ingested in food, or on food prepared in unhygienic conditions. Fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea are caused by the bacteria and the toxins they secrete. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

A sexually transmitted disease (STD) caused by a bacterium, with symptoms of a thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis and pain on urinating. It is spread by sexual contact. It was easily treated with the antibiotic penicillin until many resistant strains appeared. The spread can be controlled by treatment with antibiotics or the use of a barrier method of contraception such as a condom.

A fungal disease where purple or black spots develop on leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. It affects the growth of the plant as photosynthesis is reduced. It is spread in the environment by water or wind, and can be treated by using fungicides and/or removing and destroying the affected leaves.
The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. Malaria causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal.

An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without being the pathogen itself. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito, so the spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.
non-specific defence systems of the human body

Defences that act against pathogens in general rather than one particular pathogen: the skin acts as a barrier; the nose has hairs and mucus that trap particles from the air; the trachea and bronchi produce mucus that traps pathogens and have cilia that waft the mucus away from the lungs; the stomach produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.
The body system that tries to destroy a pathogen if that pathogen enters the body, after the non-specific defences have been passed.
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: the white blood cell takes the pathogen into itself and digests it.

One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antibodies against the pathogen. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies.
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antitoxins, which counteract the toxins produced by bacteria.

Introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection.
immunising a large proportion of the population
Vaccinating a large proportion of a population reduces the spread of a pathogen, because there are far fewer people the pathogen can infect and pass through.

A medicine, such as penicillin, that helps to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. It is important that specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.

A strain of bacteria that is not killed by an antibiotic. The use of antibiotics has greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but the emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern.

Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves. The painkiller aspirin originates from willow. Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.
The three things for which new drugs are extensively tested: toxicity, which is how harmful the drug is; efficacy, which is how well it works; and dose, which is how much of it should be given.
The stage of drug development done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals, before the drug is given to people.

The stage of drug development that uses healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial. If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out to find the optimum dose for the drug. In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo.

An antibody produced from a single clone of cells. Monoclonal antibodies are specific to one binding site on one protein antigen, and so are able to target a specific chemical or specific cells in the body.

The cell made when mouse lymphocytes, which have been stimulated to make a particular antibody, are combined with a particular kind of tumour cell. The hybridoma cell can both divide and make the antibody.
Cloning and purification of the antibody
Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells that all produce the same antibody. A large amount of the antibody can then be collected and purified.
Monoclonal antibodies in diagnosis and research

Uses that depend on the antibody binding to one specific antigen: for diagnosis, such as in pregnancy tests; in laboratories to measure the levels of hormones and other chemicals in blood, or to detect pathogens; and in research to locate or identify specific molecules in a cell or tissue by binding to them with a fluorescent dye.

For cancer, the monoclonal antibody can be bound to a radioactive substance, a toxic drug or a chemical which stops cells growing and dividing. It delivers the substance to the cancer cells without harming other cells in the body.

Plant diseases can be detected from observable signs on the plant: stunted growth, spots on leaves, areas of decay (rot), growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration, and the presence of pests.

Once a disease has been detected, it can be identified by reference to a gardening manual or website, by taking infected plants to a laboratory to identify the pathogen, or by using testing kits that contain monoclonal antibodies.

A viral pathogen of plants. It gives a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves; because the discoloured areas contain less chlorophyll, less photosynthesis occurs and the growth of the plant is affected.
A fungal disease of roses. Purple or black spots develop on the leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early, so less photosynthesis occurs and the growth of the plant is affected.
Insects that infest plants and feed on them, taking dissolved sugars and other nutrients from the plant and so weakening it. Aphids are insects, not pathogens.
Nitrate ions are needed by a plant for protein synthesis and therefore for growth. A plant grown in soil short of nitrate ions shows stunted growth.
Magnesium ions are needed by a plant to make chlorophyll. A plant short of magnesium ions cannot make enough chlorophyll and shows chlorosis, in which the leaves turn yellow.
Structures that resist invasion of microorganisms: cellulose cell walls, a tough waxy cuticle on leaves, and layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees) which fall off.
Substances a plant produces to defend itself: antibacterial chemicals, and poisons to deter herbivores.
Adaptations that protect a plant from animals: thorns and hairs which deter animals, leaves which droop or curl when touched, and mimicry to trick animals.

The reaction represented by the equation carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen, which takes place in the chloroplasts. Written with chemical symbols, CO2 and H2O react to form C6H12O6 and O2.
A reaction that takes in energy from its surroundings. Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.
The amount of product formed in a given time, calculated by dividing the amount of product by the time taken, for example bubbles of oxygen released per minute or cm3 of oxygen produced per minute.

The factor that is controlling the rate of photosynthesis at that moment, so that increasing it increases the rate. Temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll all affect the rate of photosynthesis.

Temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll interact, and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. On a graph, the limiting factor is the one which, when increased on its own, raises the rate further.
inverse square law and light intensity

Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source. Doubling the distance reduces the light intensity to one quarter, and halving the distance increases it four times.

Growers enhance temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration in greenhouses to gain the maximum rate of photosynthesis. The cost of enhancing the conditions must be less than the extra income gained, so limiting factors are important in the economics of greenhouse growing.

The glucose produced in photosynthesis may be used for respiration, converted into insoluble starch for storage, used to produce fat or oil for storage, used to produce cellulose which strengthens the cell wall, or used to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
Ions that are absorbed from the soil and used by plants, together with the glucose produced in photosynthesis, to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
An exothermic reaction which is continuously occurring in living cells, transferring energy from glucose. The energy transferred supplies all the energy needed for living processes.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings. Because respiration is exothermic, respiring cells and tissues get warmer as energy is transferred.
Uses of the energy transferred by respiration

Organisms need energy for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for movement, and for keeping warm. The energy transferred is also used for the continual enzyme controlled processes of metabolism that synthesise new molecules.
Respiration in cells that takes place using oxygen. Glucose is completely oxidised, so a relatively large amount of energy is transferred compared with anaerobic respiration.
Respiration in cells that takes place without oxygen, to transfer energy. The products differ from those of aerobic respiration and much less energy is transferred.
Aerobic respiration is represented by the equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
C6H12O6 is glucose, O2 is oxygen, CO2 is carbon dioxide and H2O is water. These symbols are used in place of the words in the equation for aerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation: glucose → lactic acid. No carbon dioxide or water is produced by this reaction.
In anaerobic respiration the oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells
Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells is represented by the equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.

Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells. It has economic importance in the manufacture of bread, where the carbon dioxide makes the dough rise, and of alcoholic drinks, which contain the ethanol produced.
Response of the body to exercise
During exercise the human body reacts to the increased demand for energy. The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.
Muscle fatigue and oxygen debt in exercise

If insufficient oxygen is supplied, anaerobic respiration takes place in muscles. The incomplete oxidation of glucose causes a build up of lactic acid and creates an oxygen debt. During long periods of vigorous activity muscles become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently.
Oxygen debt and the fate of lactic acid

Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.

The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body. The energy transferred by respiration in cells is used by the organism for these continual enzyme controlled processes, which synthesise new molecules.

Metabolism includes: conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids; the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins; respiration; and the breakdown of excess proteins to form urea for excretion.
Small molecules used in synthesis and breakdown

Sugars are used to synthesise carbohydrates such as starch, glycogen and cellulose; amino acids are used to synthesise proteins, and excess protein is broken down to form urea; glycerol and fatty acids are used to synthesise lipids. Breakdown of these larger molecules releases the same small molecules again.
The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes.
A cell that detects a stimulus, which is a change in the environment.
A part of the body, such as the brain, spinal cord or pancreas, that receives and processes information from receptors.
A muscle or gland that brings about a response which restores the optimum level.
internal conditions controlled in the human body
In the human body, the conditions controlled by homeostasis include blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels.
The system of receptors, neurones and the central nervous system that enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour.
A cell or structure that detects a stimulus, for example the light receptors in the retina or the temperature receptors in the skin.
A nerve cell that carries information as electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, and from the central nervous system to effectors.
The brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors to the information it receives from receptors.
A structure that brings about the response. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
The sequence stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response, which describes how the body detects and responds to a change.
An automatic and rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
The pathway taken by an impulse in a reflex action: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the CNS → motor neurone → effector.
The junction between two neurones. A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.
The organ that controls complex behaviour. It is made of billions of interconnected neurones and has different regions that carry out different functions.
The outer, folded region of the brain, responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.
The region at the back and base of the brain, responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance.
The region of the brain stem that controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.
The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye; the cornea is the transparent front part of that layer, which refracts light entering the eye.
The coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil, and so controls how much light enters the eye.
The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour; the optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
A ring of muscle and the ligaments that attach it to the lens. Together they change the shape of the lens during accommodation.
The process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.
A defect of the eye in which rays of light from a distant object focus in front of the retina. It is generally treated with a concave spectacle lens that makes the rays focus on the retina.
A defect of the eye in which rays of light focus behind the retina. It is generally treated with a convex spectacle lens that refracts the rays so that they focus on the retina.

Spectacle lenses refract light rays so that they focus on the retina. New technologies include hard and soft contact lenses, laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea, and a replacement lens in the eye.

The centre in the brain that monitors and controls body temperature. It contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood and receives nervous impulses from temperature receptors in the skin.
The widening of blood vessels supplying the skin when body temperature is too high, which, with sweat produced from the sweat glands, causes a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.
The narrowing of blood vessels supplying the skin when body temperature is too low, which reduces the transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.
The system composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A chemical secreted by a gland directly into the bloodstream; the blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.
Compared to the nervous system, the effects brought about by the endocrine system are slower but act for longer.

A 'master gland' in the brain which secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions; these hormones in turn act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.

On a diagram of the human body: the pituitary gland is in the brain; the thyroid is in the neck; the adrenal glands are on top of the kidneys; the pancreas lies behind the stomach; the ovaries are in the lower abdomen; the testes are below the abdomen in the scrotum.
The gland that monitors and controls blood glucose concentration by producing hormones.
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too high; it causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.
The storage substance made in liver and muscle cells, where excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
A disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels and normally treated with insulin injections.
A disorder in which the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; a carbohydrate controlled diet and an exercise regime are common treatments, and obesity is a risk factor.
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too low; it causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.

Control in which a level that has moved away from normal brings about a response that returns it to normal; it controls blood glucose through insulin and glucagon, the water level through ADH, and thyroxine levels.
If body cells lose or gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently.
Water leaves the body via the lungs during exhalation, and there is no control over this loss.
The liquid lost from the skin, containing water, ions and urea; there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the skin.
A waste substance lost from the skin in sweat and removed, with excess water and ions, via the kidneys in the urine.

The process in the liver in which excess amino acids from the digestion of dietary protein are deaminated to form ammonia; ammonia is toxic and so it is immediately converted to urea for safe excretion.
The first stage by which the kidneys produce urine, in which the blood is filtered.
The taking back into the blood of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water after the blood has been filtered by the kidneys.

The hormone that controls the water level in the body; it is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated and acts on the kidney tubules, making them more permeable so that more water is reabsorbed back into the blood.

People who suffer from kidney failure may be treated by organ transplant or by using kidney dialysis; in dialysis the blood flows next to a dialysis fluid that contains no urea but the same concentration of useful substances as normal blood, so urea passes out of the blood while glucose and useful ions are not lost.
The features that develop during puberty, caused by reproductive hormones.
The main female reproductive hormone, produced in the ovary; with progesterone it is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
The release of an egg from the ovary; from puberty eggs begin to mature and one is released approximately every 28 days.
The main male reproductive hormone, produced by the testes; it stimulates sperm production.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which stimulates the release of the egg.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which, with oestrogen, is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.

Methods of controlling fertility that use hormones: oral contraceptives that contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature; and injection, implant or skin patch of slow release progesterone to inhibit the maturation and release of eggs for a number of months or years. Some intrauterine devices also release a hormone.

Methods of controlling fertility that do not use hormones: barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms which prevent the sperm reaching an egg; intrauterine devices which prevent the implantation of an embryo; spermicidal agents which kill or disable sperm; abstaining from intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct; and surgical methods of male and female sterilisation.
A drug containing FSH and LH given to a woman to treat infertility, after which she may become pregnant in the normal way.

Fertility treatment in which a mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs; the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory, the fertilised eggs develop into embryos, and at the stage when they are tiny balls of cells one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus. It is very emotionally and physically stressful, the success rates are not high, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.

A hormone produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for 'flight or fight'.
A hormone from the thyroid gland which stimulates the basal metabolic rate and plays an important role in growth and development; its level is controlled by negative feedback.
A chemical produced by a plant that coordinates and controls growth and the plant's responses to stimuli such as light and gravity.
The growth response of a plant to light. A shoot lit from one side bends towards the light because auxin is unequally distributed, giving unequal growth rates on the two sides.
The growth response of a plant to gravity. Roots grow towards gravity and shoots grow away from it, because auxin is unequally distributed and causes unequal growth rates.

A plant hormone whose unequal distribution causes unequal growth rates in plant roots and shoots. Where auxin collects in a shoot the growth rate increases; where it collects in a root the growth rate is reduced, so the shoot or root bends.
Plant hormones that are important in initiating seed germination.
A plant hormone that controls cell division and the ripening of fruits.
Commercial use of plant growth hormones

Plant growth hormones are used in agriculture and horticulture to control plant growth: auxins as weed killers, as rooting powders and for promoting growth in tissue culture; ethene in the food industry to control ripening of fruit during storage and transport; gibberellins to end seed dormancy, promote flowering and increase fruit size.

The type of cell division that leads to non-identical cells being formed. It takes place in the reproductive organs to form gametes, and all the gametes produced are genetically different from each other.

The type of cell division that leads to identical cells being formed. It is the only division involved in asexual reproduction, and it is the division by which the new cell formed at fertilisation increases the number of cells.
Reproduction involving the joining (fusion) of male and female gametes. Because there is mixing of genetic information from two parents, it leads to variety in the offspring.

A sex cell that joins with another gamete at fertilisation. In animals the gametes are sperm and egg cells; in flowering plants they are pollen and egg cells. A gamete contains a single set of chromosomes.
Reproduction involving only one parent and no fusion of gametes. There is no mixing of genetic information, only mitosis is involved, and the offspring are genetically identical to the parent.
An offspring that is genetically identical to its parent. Clones are produced by asexual reproduction because only mitosis is involved and there is no mixing of genetic information.

Cells in the reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes. Copies of the genetic information are made, then the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes and all genetically different from each other.
The joining of two gametes, which restores the normal number of chromosomes. Meiosis halves the chromosome number in the gametes, so fertilisation of two gametes brings the full number back.
After fertilisation the new cell divides by mitosis so the number of cells increases. As the embryo develops these cells differentiate, becoming specialised for different jobs.

Sexual reproduction produces variation in the offspring. If the environment changes, variation gives a survival advantage by natural selection. Natural selection can also be speeded up by humans in selective breeding to increase food production.

Asexual reproduction needs only one parent, so it is more time and energy efficient as there is no need to find a mate. It is faster than sexual reproduction and many identical offspring can be produced when conditions are favourable.

Some organisms reproduce by both methods depending on the circumstances. Malarial parasites reproduce asexually in the human host but sexually in the mosquito; many fungi reproduce asexually by spores but also sexually to give variation; many plants produce seeds sexually but also reproduce asexually by runners, such as strawberry plants, or bulb division, such as daffodils.
The chemical of which the genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed. DNA is a polymer made up of two strands forming a double helix, and it is contained in structures called chromosomes.
A structure in the nucleus that contains the DNA. Genes are carried as small sections of DNA along a chromosome.
A small section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
The entire genetic material of an organism. The whole human genome has now been studied and this will have great importance for medicine in the future.
Importance of understanding the human genome

Understanding the human genome matters for three reasons: the search for genes linked to different types of disease, the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders, and its use in tracing human migration patterns from the past.

The repeating unit from which the DNA polymer is made. Each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar, and DNA is made from four different nucleotides.
DNA contains four bases, A, C, G and T. One of these bases is attached to the sugar of each nucleotide, and the order of the bases carries the code.
A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid. The order of bases therefore controls the order in which amino acids are assembled to produce a particular protein.
The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections. Attached to each sugar is one of the four bases.
In the complementary strands of the double helix a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand, and a T to an A.
Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template. Carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.
When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape. This unique shape enables proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or forming structures in the body such as collagen.
A change in DNA structure. Mutations occur continuously, and most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.
Effect of a mutation on a protein
A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape. An enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site, or a structural protein may lose its strength.
Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Non-coding parts of DNA can switch genes on and off, so variations in these areas of DNA may affect how genes are expressed.
One of the different forms a gene may have. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans.
An allele that is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present, and therefore no dominant allele is present.
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are the same.
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are different.
The alleles present in an organism. The genotype operates at a molecular level to develop characteristics.
The characteristics that the genotype develops and that are expressed in the organism.
Most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting, rather than a single gene, so most phenotype features are not the result of single gene inheritance.

A diagram used to set out a genetic cross by combining the alleles carried by the gametes of each parent. The outcome can be expressed using direct proportion or simple ratios, and gives the probability of each genotype rather than a guaranteed result.

Disorders caused by the inheritance of certain alleles. Polydactyly, having extra fingers or toes, is caused by a dominant allele. Cystic fibrosis, a disorder of cell membranes, is caused by a recessive allele.

Screening embryos for the alleles that cause inherited disorders. It raises economic, social and ethical issues about which students should make informed judgements when given appropriate information.

Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes. 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex: in females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX) and in males they are different (XY).
The characteristics of an organism. The phenotype develops as a result of the genome of the organism and its interaction with the environment.

Differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population. Variation may be due to the genes they have inherited (genetic causes), the conditions in which they have developed (environmental causes), or a combination of genes and the environment.

A change in the DNA of an organism. All variants arise from mutations, and mutations occur continuously. Very rarely a mutation will lead to a new phenotype, and if that new phenotype is suited to an environmental change it can lead to a relatively rapid change in the species.
Effect of mutations on the phenotype

There is usually extensive genetic variation within a population of a species. Of the variants that arise from mutations, most have no effect on the phenotype, some influence phenotype and very few determine phenotype.
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of a new species.

The process by which variants that give rise to phenotypes best suited to their environment are the most likely to survive and to breed successfully, so that the genes for these characteristics are passed on to the next generation.
Theory of evolution by natural selection
The theory that all species of living things have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
Two populations of one species have formed two new species when they become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

The process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics. Parents with the desired characteristic are chosen from a mixed population and bred together; from the offspring, those with the desired characteristic are bred together, and this continues over many generations until all the offspring show the desired characteristic. Humans have done this for thousands of years, since they first bred food crops from wild plants and domesticated animals.

The characteristic that humans select for in selective breeding, chosen for usefulness or appearance. Examples are disease resistance in food crops, animals which produce more meat or milk, domestic dogs with a gentle nature, and large or unusual flowers.
Breeding from closely related individuals, which selective breeding can lead to. Some breeds produced in this way are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects.

A process which involves modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic. Genes from the chromosomes of humans and other organisms can be 'cut out' and transferred to cells of other organisms.

Crops that have had their genes modified by genetic engineering. GM crops include ones that are resistant to insect attack or to herbicides, and GM crops generally show increased yields. Plant crops have also been genetically engineered to be resistant to diseases or to produce bigger better fruits. Concerns about GM crops include the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects, and some people feel that the effects of eating GM crops on human health have not been fully explored.
Bacterial cells that have been genetically engineered to produce useful substances, such as human insulin to treat diabetes.
Modern medical research is exploring the possibility of genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.

In genetic engineering, the structure that carries the required gene into cells, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus. Enzymes are used to isolate the required gene, the gene is inserted into the vector, and the vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells. Genes are transferred to the cells of animals, plants or microorganisms at an early stage in their development so that they develop with the desired characteristics.
Using small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants. This is important for preserving rare plant species or commercially in nurseries.
An older, but simple, method used by gardeners to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant.
Splitting apart cells from a developing animal embryo before they become specialised, then transplanting the identical embryos into host mothers.

A process in which the nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell and the nucleus from an adult body cell, such as a skin cell, is inserted into the egg cell. An electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide to form an embryo, and these embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell. When the embryo has developed into a ball of cells it is inserted into the womb of an adult female to continue its development.

The process by which individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, so that the characteristics which have enabled these individuals to survive are then passed on to the next generation. Charles Darwin proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection as a result of observations on a round the world expedition, backed by years of experimentation and discussion and linked to developing knowledge of geology and fossils.

The differences between individuals of the same species. Individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic, and this variation is already present in the population before natural selection acts on it.
The book in which Darwin published his ideas about evolution by natural selection in 1859. There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas.

The theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted because the theory challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants that live on Earth, because there was insufficient evidence at the time the theory was published to convince many scientists, and because the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.

Another theory of how species change, proposed by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, based mainly on the idea that changes that occur in an organism during its lifetime can be inherited. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.

The scientist who independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. He published joint writings with Darwin in 1858 which prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species (1859) the following year. Wallace worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory and is best known for his work on warning colouration in animals and his theory of speciation.
The formation of new species. Alfred Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation, but more evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.
Steps that give rise to a new species

Populations of a species become isolated from one another and experience different conditions. There is variation within each population, and natural selection means that individuals with the characteristics most suited to their own environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully and pass those characteristics on. Over many generations the two populations become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so they are two species.

In the mid-19th Century Gregor Mendel carried out breeding experiments on plants. One of his observations was that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.
Why Mendel's discovery was not recognised in his lifetime

Mendel worked in the mid-19th Century, before the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division had been observed, so there was no known structure that could carry his 'units'. The significance of his discovery was therefore not appreciated by scientists at the time and was only recognised after his death.

In the late 19th Century the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed. In the early 20th Century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways, and this led to the idea that the 'units', now called genes, were located on chromosomes.
Structure of DNA and gene theory
In the mid-20th Century the structure of DNA was determined and the mechanism of gene function was worked out. This scientific work by many scientists led to the gene theory being developed.

Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available as it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes. There is further evidence in the fossil record and in the knowledge of how resistance to antibiotics evolves in bacteria. Because of this evidence the theory of evolution by natural selection is now widely accepted, which is the impact these ideas have had on biology.
The 'remains' of organisms from millions of years ago, which are found in rocks.

Fossils may be formed from parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent, when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay, or as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.
Gaps in the early fossil record

Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind. What traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity. This is why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth.

A diagram, built from evidence such as the fossil record, in which a branch point shows a common ancestor shared by the organisms on the branches above it. Evolutionary trees and other charts, graphs and tables let us learn from fossils how much or how little different organisms have changed as life developed on Earth.
Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.

A species may become extinct because of changes to the environment over geological time, new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, or a single catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption or a collision with an asteroid.
Bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.

Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains. Some strains might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises. The resistant strain will then spread because people are not immune to it and there is no effective treatment.
A strain of bacteria which is resistant to antibiotics.
Reducing the development of resistant strains

To reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains, doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections; patients should complete their course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains; and the agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted.
The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow. It is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains.
The traditional system of classification, developed by Carl Linnaeus, in which living things are classified into groups depending on their structure and characteristics.

The groups Linnaeus classified living things into: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Kingdom is the largest group and species the smallest, so organisms placed in the same genus share more characteristics than organisms placed only in the same class.
The system used to name organisms, in which an organism is given a two-part name made up of its genus followed by its species, for example Panthera leo.

Classification systems proposed after Linnaeus. As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.

The system developed by Carl Woese, due to evidence available from chemical analysis, in which organisms are divided into Archaea (primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukaryota (which includes protists, fungi, plants and animals).
A method used by scientists to show how they believe organisms are related, drawn using current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.
The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
The place where an organism lives. It supplies the conditions and the materials the organism needs from its surroundings in order to survive and reproduce.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat. A population is the level of organisation between the individual organism and the community.
The populations of all the different species living together in a habitat. Within a community each species depends on the other species living there.

Organisms of the same or different species competing for the same resource where the supply is limited. Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.
Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. If one species is removed it can affect the whole community.
A community where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.

A non-living factor which can affect a community. The abiotic factors are: light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; oxygen levels for aquatic animals.

A living factor which can affect a community. The biotic factors are: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another so the numbers are no longer sufficient to breed.
A feature that an organism has which enables it to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.

The three types of adaptation. Structural adaptations are features of the organism's body, such as its shape or covering. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does. Functional adaptations are the ways processes inside the organism's body work.
An organism that lives in an environment that is very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.
Materials required to survive and reproduce

To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there, for example light, water and mineral ions for a plant, and food from other organisms for an animal.

The organism at the start of a food chain, which synthesises molecules. It is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis. Photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth.

A way of representing feeding relationships within a community. All food chains begin with a producer, which is eaten by a primary consumer, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers and then tertiary consumers.
An organism that eats producers. Primary consumers may in turn be eaten by secondary consumers.
An organism that eats primary consumers. Secondary consumers may in turn be eaten by tertiary consumers.
Consumers that kill and eat other animals are predators, and those eaten are prey. In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles.

A square frame of known area placed on the ground, used by ecologists to determine the abundance of a species by counting the organisms inside it. Quadrats are placed at random positions so that the sample represents the whole area.
A line marked across a habitat, along which quadrats are placed at intervals. Transects are used by ecologists to determine how the distribution of a species changes across an ecosystem.

The total of all the readings divided by the number of readings, used to summarise the abundance of a species from repeated quadrat counts. It differs from the median, which is the middle value when the readings are put in order, and the mode, which is the most common value.
The non-living (abiotic) and living (biotic) parts of an ecosystem. Many different materials cycle through the abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem.
All materials in the living world are recycled to provide the building blocks for future organisms, rather than being used once and lost.
The cycle that returns carbon from organisms to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, to be used by plants in photosynthesis.
The cycle that provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas. Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.

The breakdown of dead organisms and waste biological material by microorganisms, which returns carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the soil. The rate of decay is affected by temperature, water and the availability of oxygen.
Decay that takes place in the absence of oxygen. Anaerobic decay produces methane gas, and biogas generators can be used to produce methane gas as a fuel.

The material produced when gardeners and farmers provide optimum conditions for rapid decay of waste biological material. The compost is used as a natural fertiliser for growing garden plants or crops.

Where a species is found within an ecosystem. Environmental changes affect the distribution of species; these changes include temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases, and they may be seasonal, geographic or caused by human interaction.
The variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem.
Biodiversity and the stability of ecosystems
A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.

The future of the human species on Earth relies on us maintaining a good level of biodiversity. Many human activities are reducing biodiversity and only recently have measures been taken to try to stop this reduction.
Human population growth and standard of living

Rapid growth in the human population and an increase in the standard of living mean that increasingly more resources are used and more waste is produced. Unless waste and chemical materials are properly handled, more pollution will be caused.

Pollution can occur in water, from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals; in air, from smoke and acidic gases; and on land, from landfill and from toxic chemicals. Pollution kills plants and animals which can reduce biodiversity.
Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.

The destruction of peat bogs, and other areas of peat to produce garden compost, reduces the area of this habitat and thus the variety of different plant, animal and microorganism species that live there (biodiversity).
The decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas has occurred to provide land for cattle and rice fields, and to grow crops for biofuels.
Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing, and contribute to 'global warming'.
Programmes to protect ecosystems and biodiversity

Scientists and concerned citizens have put in place programmes to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity. These include: breeding programmes for endangered species; protection and regeneration of rare habitats; reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows in agricultural areas where farmers grow only one type of crop; reduction of deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions by some governments; recycling resources rather than dumping waste in landfill.

The position an organism occupies in a food chain. Trophic levels can be represented by numbers, starting at level 1 with plants and algae; further trophic levels are numbered subsequently according to how far the organism is along the food chain.
An organism at trophic level 1. Plants and algae make their own food and are called producers.
An organism at trophic level 2. Herbivores eat plants/algae and are called primary consumers.
An organism at trophic level 3. Carnivores that eat herbivores are called secondary consumers.
An organism at trophic level 4. Carnivores that eat other carnivores are called tertiary consumers.
A carnivore with no predators. Apex predators are found at the end of a food chain.
A microorganism that breaks down dead plant and animal matter by secreting enzymes into the environment. Small soluble food molecules then diffuse into the microorganism.

A diagram constructed to represent the relative amount of biomass in each level of a food chain. Trophic level 1 is at the bottom of the pyramid, and the width of each bar represents the biomass at that level.
Transfer of light energy by producers
Producers are mostly plants and algae which transfer about 1% of the incident energy from light for photosynthesis.
Only approximately 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above it, so less biomass is available at each higher trophic level.

Biomass is lost between trophic levels because not all the ingested material is absorbed, some being egested as faeces, and because some absorbed material is lost as waste, such as carbon dioxide and water in respiration and water and urea in urine. Large amounts of glucose are used in respiration.

The biomass transferred to a trophic level expressed as a percentage or fraction of the biomass available at the level below it: biomass transferred divided by biomass available, multiplied by 100 for a percentage.
Having enough food to feed a population.

Factors that reduce the amount of food available to a population. They include: the increasing birth rate, which has threatened food security in some countries; changing diets in developed countries, which means scarce food resources are transported around the world; new pests and pathogens that affect farming; environmental changes that affect food production, such as widespread famine occurring in some countries if rains fail; the cost of agricultural inputs; and conflicts that have arisen in some parts of the world which affect the availability of water or food.
Producing food in ways that can be continued into the future without the supply running out. Sustainable methods must be found to feed all people on Earth.
Restricting energy transfer from food animals

The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment. This can be done by limiting their movement and by controlling the temperature of their surroundings, so that more of the energy in their food is used for growth.
High protein foods in animal feed
Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth, which improves the efficiency of food production.
Fish stocks in the oceans are declining. It is important to maintain fish stocks at a level where breeding continues, or certain species may disappear altogether in some areas.
Fishing quotas and control of net size

Two methods used to conserve fish stocks at a sustainable level. A fishing quota is a limit on the mass or number of a species that may be caught. Controlling net size, by setting a minimum mesh size, allows young fish to escape so that breeding continues.
Modern biotechnology techniques enable large quantities of microorganisms to be cultured for food, providing a source of protein for a growing human population.
A protein-rich food suitable for vegetarians, produced using the fungus Fusarium. The fungus is grown on glucose syrup, in aerobic conditions, and the biomass is harvested and purified.
Human insulin from a genetically modified bacterium
A genetically modified bacterium produces human insulin. When harvested and purified this is used to treat people with diabetes.
